title: The obstructed, infected kidney

header.contentArea: Urology: upper tract obstruction and sepsis
guidelineVersions: NICE NG148, Acute kidney injury: prevention, detection and management (published 18 December 2019; last updated 16 October 2024)

related.why: Applied anatomy of the kidney and ureter, relevant to how the obstruction is decompressed
History of loin pain and suspected renal colic, the presentation that can lead to this emergency

brief.scenario: Mr Michael Renshaw, 55, presents with fever, rigors and severe flank pain. Imaging shows an obstructed ureteric system.
brief.task: Discuss the diagnosis, your priorities, and how you would achieve source control.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: An infected obstructed kidney is a urological emergency: treat sepsis and decompress, in parallel, without waiting for one before the other.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Treating the infection first and planning decompression later, or trying definitive stone treatment in a septic patient.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "This is an infected obstructed upper urinary tract, potentially pyonephrosis, and it's a urological emergency."

flow: Separate decompression from definitive stone treatment

grid.label: Naming the diagnosis
grid.fail: Describes this only as a urinary tract infection or renal colic.
grid.pass: States this is an infected, obstructed upper urinary tract, potentially pyonephrosis, and a urological emergency.
grid.high: Explains why the combination of infection and obstruction, rather than either alone, makes this an emergency.

grid.label: Sepsis assessment
grid.fail: Starts antibiotics without any structured assessment.
grid.pass: Assesses for sepsis using an A-E approach, obtains cultures and starts appropriate antibiotics promptly.
grid.high: Explains cultures are taken without delaying antibiotics, since prompt treatment matters more than a perfect sample.

grid.label: Urgent urology involvement
grid.fail: Manages this alone without involving urology, or refers routinely.
grid.high: States that pyonephrosis, an obstructed solitary kidney, bilateral upper tract obstruction, or AKI caused by the obstruction all warrant immediate urological referral.

grid.label: Source control (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Treats antibiotics as sufficient on their own, or plans decompression only if antibiotics fail.
grid.pass: States the key issue is source control: the obstructed system requires urgent decompression, and antibiotics alone do not achieve this.
grid.high: States decompression should be carried out as soon as possible and within 12 hours of diagnosis when indicated for obstruction-related AKI.

grid.label: Choosing the decompression method
grid.fail: Cannot name a method of decompression.
grid.pass: States decompression can be achieved by ureteric stenting or nephrostomy, depending on the clinical and anatomical circumstances.
grid.high: Notes nephrostomy avoids instrumenting an infected, obstructed system retrogradely and is often favoured when there is doubt about safely passing a stent.

grid.label: Separating decompression from definitive treatment
grid.fail: Would perform definitive stone treatment immediately in the septic patient.
grid.pass: States definitive stone treatment is usually separate from, and comes after, emergency decompression.
grid.high: Adds that renal function and urine output are monitored in the interim, since AKI can persist after decompression.

failures.consequence: Decompression is delayed past the window in which source control is most effective.

failures.move: Treating antibiotics as sufficient on their own.
failures.consequence: The obstruction remains, and sepsis is not controlled at its source.

failures.move: Planning decompression only after antibiotics have had time to work.
failures.consequence: Delay beyond 12 hours worsens outcomes in obstruction-related AKI.

failures.move: Performing definitive stone treatment while the patient is septic.
failures.consequence: Adds procedural risk before source control and sepsis have been addressed.

recovery.line: I'd like to structure this around immediate safety, assessment, escalation and definitive management.
Yes — I'd also monitor renal function and urine output, and keep definitive stone treatment for later.

knowledge.fact: Immediate urological referral is required for pyonephrosis, an obstructed solitary kidney, bilateral upper urinary tract obstruction, or AKI caused by obstruction.
When nephrostomy or stenting is used for AKI from upper tract obstruction, decompression should be carried out as soon as possible and within 12 hours of diagnosis.
Antibiotics alone do not achieve source control; the obstructed system needs decompression. Definitive stone treatment is usually separate and later.

recall.think: An infected, obstructed kidney that antibiotics alone cannot fix.
recall.say: "This is a urological emergency — source control means decompressing the obstruction."

partner.opening: Mr Renshaw, 55, has fever, rigors and severe flank pain, with imaging showing an obstructed ureteric system. "What is the diagnosis?"

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks for observations or sepsis markers
reveals.finding: Temperature 39.1°C, heart rate 118, blood pressure 98/58, lactate 3.2.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about the imaging in more detail
reveals.finding: Moderate right hydronephrosis with a 7mm obstructing ureteric calculus; no solitary or contralateral kidney abnormality.

push.question: What are your priorities?
push.expect: A-E sepsis assessment, cultures, prompt antibiotics.

push.question: How do you achieve source control?
push.expect: Urgent decompression by stent or nephrostomy; antibiotics alone are not enough.

push.question: Is stone removal or drainage the priority?
push.expect: In the septic obstructed system, urgent drainage/source control comes first; definitive stone treatment is separate and later.

curveballs.prompt: He has only one functioning kidney.
curveballs.safeAnswer: This alone warrants immediate urological referral, regardless of severity of infection.

curveballs.prompt: The urology team asks whether to stent or nephrostomy him.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Explains the choice depends on clinical and anatomical circumstances, and nephrostomy may be preferred to avoid retrograde instrumentation of the infected system.

curveballs.prompt: He remains oliguric 24 hours after decompression.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Continues monitoring renal function and urine output, since AKI can persist after source control is achieved.
